Full recovery after a periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) usually takes about **6 to 12 months**. Most people get back to everyday activities, work or school in around **3 months**. One university hospital says it usually takes 9–12 months to feel fully recovered. Some surgeons quote a shorter range, four to six months.

**Typical timeline**

- **Hospital stay:** usually two to three days. Physical therapy starts the day after surgery. Plan on having someone take care of you 24/7 for the first week.
- **Weeks 0–6:** You walk with crutches (partial weight bearing) and keep the wound clean. The first follow-up is two weeks after surgery, then again at six weeks for X-rays.
- **Weeks 6–12:** You move to one cane or crutch as your provider instructs, and may start gentle stretching or strengthening exercises. Most people walk without crutches about eight weeks after surgery. By two to three months, most patients can put full weight on the hip and return to everyday activities.
- **About 3 months:** Many people go back to work part time or full time as tolerated. In one study, most patients returned to school and work within 12 weeks, and 55% were driving again within 6 weeks. Pain will most likely be gone within four months after the operation.
- **4–6 months:** In a study of non-athletes, patients got back to their pre-surgery activity levels in an average of 4.5 months (range 2–12 months). After six months, you may return to full activity once the bone cuts have fully healed, except for running and jumping.
- **9–12 months:** Most people feel fully recovered. High-impact sports may take longer.

**Things to keep in mind**

- **Don't rush weight bearing.** Protocols differ between surgeons. One study found that an accelerated protocol helped patients walk without support sooner (4.2 vs. 6.9 months), but postoperative pelvic fracture rates were unacceptably high with that approach.
- **Physical therapy is a big part of recovery.** It helps strengthen the muscles around the hip and pelvis and restore range of motion.
- **Your own timeline may differ.** It depends on your age, fitness, whether other procedures (like arthroscopy) were done at the same time, and how your bone heals. Your surgeon's specific instructions should come first.

Recovery time depends mostly on which surgery you have: trimming out the torn piece or stitching the tear back together. The surgeon chooses between them based on where the tear is, its pattern, and its blood supply.

**Partial meniscectomy (removing the torn part): weeks**
- According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, "A partial meniscectomy requires less time for healing — approximately 3 to 6 weeks."
- You can usually walk within days and get back to normal activity in 4–8 weeks.
- Straight-line running begins around 8–12 weeks after meniscectomy. People who play sports with cutting and pivoting, like basketball, soccer, and tennis, typically return at 3–4 months.

**Meniscus repair (stitching the tear): months**
- Rehab after a meniscus repair takes about 3 to 6 months. Hospital for Special Surgery says full recovery is typically 6 to 9 months depending on the activities of the patient.
- You'll keep weight off the leg, or only touch your toes down, for 4–6 weeks, depending on how complex the repair is.
- Running starts around 4–6 months, and cutting and pivoting sports usually resume at 6–9 months after repair.
- It takes longer because the stitched meniscus tissue has to actually heal, which happens slowly, and it needs protecting in the meantime.

**Driving and work**
- **Driving:** Typically one to two weeks after a meniscectomy on the right knee, sooner for the left knee if you drive an automatic, and four to six weeks or more after a repair.
- **Work:** Many people go back to desk work early, including after a repair if they can keep the leg raised and manage the commute. Jobs where you stand usually take two to six weeks after a meniscectomy and two to three months after a repair.

**Why the slower option is often recommended anyway:** Repair keeps the meniscus and lowers the risk of arthritis, but recovery takes longer. Removal is faster to recover from but may raise the risk of joint wear over time.

Your own timeline will depend on your tear, your age, how active you are, and how closely you follow physical therapy, so your surgeon's plan comes first.

Typical recovery after **rotator cuff surgery** is:

- **Sling:** about **4–6 weeks** ([fhft.nhs.uk](https://www.fhft.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-library/guidelines-patients-rotator-cuff-repair/submit/7561?utm_source=openai))

- **Stronger attachment to bone:** about **3 months** ([hopkinsmedicine.org](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/failed-rotator-cuff-repairs?utm_source=openai))
- **Many daily activities improve:** around **6–12 weeks** for light use, but with restrictions ([fhft.nhs.uk](https://www.fhft.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-library/guidelines-patients-rotator-cuff-repair/submit/7561?utm_source=openai))
- **Full recovery:** often **4–6 months**, but many patients take **6–9 months**, and some need up to **12 months** to feel close to normal again. ([hopkinsmedicine.org](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/rotator-cuff-repair?utm_source=openai))

A simple way to think about it:
- **Desk-type work:** often **1–2 weeks**, sometimes longer if pain or sling use is a problem.
- **Driving:** usually **after sling use ends** and when your surgeon clears you.
- **Manual labor / lifting / sports:** often **4–6 months or more**. This varies a lot. ([hopkinsmedicine.org](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/rotator-cuff-repair?utm_source=openai))

It depends on:
- size of the tear
- arthroscopic vs open surgery
- your age and health
- whether this is a revision surgery

Full recovery from rotator cuff surgery usually takes **about 6 to 12 months**. How long it takes for you depends mostly on how big the tear was.

**By tear size (Hospital for Special Surgery):**
- Small tears: about four months for full recovery. Large tears: about six months.
- Severe, massive tears: anywhere from 6 to 12 months.

**Typical timeline:**
- **Weeks 0–6:** You wear a sling, the arm is only moved for you (passive motion), and the goal is protecting the repair. Physical therapy usually starts about one week after surgery.
- **Weeks 6–12:** You start moving the arm on your own again. The tendon takes six to eight weeks to heal to the bone.
- **Months 3–6:** Strengthening. Most people can return to most activities about 12 weeks after surgery, but vigorous sports may be off-limits for four to six months.
- **Months 6–12 and later:** Strength keeps coming back, especially after larger tears. Strength and comfort often keep improving for 18 to 24 months after surgery.

**Other milestones:**
- **Desk work:** often within 1–2 weeks, while still in the sling
- **Driving:** commonly around 6–8 weeks
- **Manual labor:** anywhere from 3–4 months after surgery

**Why it's slow:** The surgeon reattaches the torn tendon to the bone with suture anchors, but the tendon takes months, not weeks, to grow back into the bone. If you push it too early, the repair can fail, so the sling and the "no active lifting" rules in the first phase aren't optional.

Your own timeline will also depend on your age, the quality of the tissue, your general health, and how closely you stick to physical therapy. Follow the plan your surgeon gives you.
